source.version: Journal version of record: Research Policy 55 (2026) 105597; received 30 May 2024, revised 30 June 2026, accepted 7 August 2026, available online 14 August 2026; open access CC BY (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: Searching together: Human–AI complementarities in innovation search

supplement.holds: No supplement. Appendix 1 (interviewee list) and Appendix 2 (secondary data sources) are in this PDF, p. 14-15. Data availability: 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' (p. 15)

paper_design_summary: An exploratory qualitative study based on 41 semi-structured interviews with employees of an AI search firm ('Firm AI') and with innovation managers at client and non-client organizations (27 companies), plus 64 secondary articles about AI search tools. The authors code the interviews with the Gioia grounded-theory method and derive three human-AI 'relational dialectics' in innovation search. No one is assigned to AI, and no creative output is produced or scored.

studies.label: Qualitative interview study of AI use in innovation search

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned. Interviewees were chosen by purposeful and network sampling.
assignment.quote: We used an exploratory qualitative research design to identify emerging complementarities between humans and AI in innovation search.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3 Method; sampling in Section 3.1, p. 4-5

participants.exclusions: Not applicable. The paper reports 41 interviews (1422 min) and does not state a count of distinct interviewees. Appendix 1 lists 39 rows numbered 1-41 (numbers 4 and 13 absent), with two interviewees in one row (M17A/B) and two rows marked '2 rounds' (F1, M6).
participants.who: Employees of Firm AI (F1-F5) and innovation, R&D, and technology-scouting managers and staff at 25 client organizations and one non-client organization (M1-M34) in manufacturing, chemicals, food, energy, IT, and other sectors.
participants.country: Europe (mainly Netherlands, Germany, Finland), United States, UK, Saudi Arabia
participants.quote: In total, we conducted 41 interviews, amounting to 1422 min (see Appendix 1), with an average duration of 35 min per interview.

ai_tool.name_model: Alpha AI (Firm AI's NLP search system); also Azure OpenAI service, Amazon Kendra, Glean chat, and ChatGPT discussed by interviewees and in secondary data
ai_tool.how_used: AI-powered search over scientific publications, patents, and company websites in firms' innovation search; interviewees describe their own use.

task.description: Innovation search in firms (finding technologies, solutions, and partners), as described by interviewees. No task was set by the researchers.

company_involvement.description: No company funded or co-authored the work; the authors declare no competing interests (p. 14). The research setting is a European AI search firm ('Firm AI') and its client network, which supplied interviewees (p. 4).
company_involvement.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 14, Declaration of competing interest

eligibility.reason: Qualitative interview study (41 interviews; p. 5, Appendix 1 p. 14). No random assignment, no creative output scored, and no diversity, similarity, novelty, or originality outcome, so it is not observational context either. Belongs in the screening report as out of scope.

one_line_finding: From 41 interviews across 27 organizations, the authors identify three human-AI dialectics in innovation search (human-centered vs boundary-spanning search, contextualizing vs de-contextualizing, judging vs envisaging) and argue they expand rationality and reduce biases; no quantitative outcome is reported (p. 5, p. 11 Table 2).
notes: Abstract says data come from 27 companies; Section 3.1 says 25 large client organizations plus Firm AI plus one non-client organization. The paper cites Doshi and Hauser (2024) only in limitations (p. 13). The data collection started in early 2022, before ChatGPT; generative AI is one of several AI tools discussed.
